column1: Dorotape is the home of unique, vibrant, and colourful high-quality self-adhesive films. As a trusted UK distributor for leading global brands, including ASLAN, Poli-Tape, Fedrigoni (Ritrama), Nekoosa (R-Tape), Neschen, Kernow and Cover Styl', we pride ourselves on offering one of the widest ranges of functional and decorative films available.

We’re proudly independent, which means we have our pick of the most innovative and dynamic suppliers and materials. Our vast portfolio includes self-adhesive vinyl and films for sign making, large format digital printing and stencil masking as well as heat activated adhesive films for garment decoration and a wide range of double-sided tapes.

We have the enviable reputation for being one of the UK’s main suppliers of metallised and dichroic films, but also focus heavily on premium quality coloured vinyl, glass manifestation films as well as printable materials for wall, floor and window graphics. We also have an expanding range of eco-products too, including films made from post-consumer recycled plastic and other PVC-free alternatives.

Our broad portfolio of materials allows us to work with a vast range of businesses and industries. From art installations to aircraft assembly, we wouldn’t be exaggerating if we said, and everything in between!

What we do and how we do it so well
Well, for a start it is fair to say that we are a focused team who are dedicated to offering a high level of service and who understand the importance of getting things right first time.

Sounds pretty easy eh? But in an industry that works to very tight deadlines it is even more important to maintain that attention to detail and we are proud of the reputation we have built up over the 25 years of supplying the industry.
How things move on while some things never change

We have come a long way from our humble beginnings, supplying just a few tapes back in the late Eighties when you could buy a pint for less than a pound. Since then we have continued to expand and invest in the latest technology and equipment. After out growing a number of different premises we now operate from a recently modernised, fully equipped office and warehouse in the heart of England. This means we are in the enviable position of having easy and fast access to all corners of the UK.

We are a dynamic, innovative company and we are passionate about what we do. Yes, that is a bit of a cliché but we enjoy putting all of our knowledge and experience in all aspects of the display industry to good use by building close working relationships and collaborating with our customers. We can offer assistance in every aspect of the process from design to production and installation.

We also work closely with our manufacturing partners to research and develop new adhesives, colours and finishes . This enables us to offer you the very latest innovations in product technology whilst never forgetting the old fashioned values of customer service and fair dealing that we are synonymous with.
All this experience means we understand the products we sell. Our team of product specialists can advise which materials are right for the job as well as point out their limitations too.

As one of the UK’s leading suppliers of self-adhesive films we are proud to still be completely independent, which means that we are not limited to only supplying just one brand. This enables us to select the best materials from the world's leading manufacturers and put together a product portfolio that's second to none.

Our product range comprises of a huge array of top quality self-adhesive vinyl and films for sign making, large format digital printing and stencil masking as well as heat activated adhesive films for garment decoration and a wide range of double-sided tapes. We are particularly well known for supplying speciality self-adhesive films such as Metallised and Dichroic Films, Glass Manifestation Films as well as Printable materials for Wall, Floor and Window Graphics.

By choosing from our specially selected product range you can have the confidence of knowing you are using products that have not only been designed and tested to perform, but they will also fit within your budget.
This broad portfolio of materials enables us to operate in a number of creative industry sectors as well as in a more industrial production environment :
• Exhibitions, Festivals and other indoor and outdoor Leisure and Entertainment venues
• Architectural installations and other Surface Covering for renovations

We understand that sometimes during the creative process, a specific colour, finish or texture may be requested that is not available 'off the shelf'. To address this, we offer a bespoke service for our customers where, by using state of the art in house technology, we can produce something to match these exact requirements.

We hope, whether you are a Signmaker, Production Manager, Project Manager or Designer or if you work for a Creative Agency or Local Authority, that you find our website full of creative and functional products that will inspire you to design and build exceptional displays and signage.
Please feel free to contact us at any time.

>Brexit and the effect on our industry going forward

column1: As you have probably seen in the news in the last few days, there is a strong possibility that the UK will leave the EU with effect from 01.01.2021 without an agreed trade deal in place.

Of course, we have been aware of the situation and the question mark hanging over the final decision for some time. We have taken steps to increase our stock holding in the run up to the end of the year so that we have a buffer in case of extended delays at the Channel ports. We are also working closely with our manufacturing partners in Europe to make sure that there are no material shortages going forward.

The likely ‘No Deal’ situation that we find ourselves in means that the UK will operate on World Trade Organisation terms and as a result, there would be import duties levied on all self-adhesive films and other products that we bring into the UK from the EU as well as increased administration costs relating to these imports.
As I am sure you will appreciate, if this happens it would be impossible for us to operate without passing on these additional costs and they would be reflected in our pricing structure for 2021.
If you would like any clarification, please do not hesitate to contact us.

column1: Now that we find ourselves in Tier 4 and another National lockdown, we are tightening up our protection levels. We are still open for business but request that customers are mindful of the fact that we might be operating with fewer staff and that orders might take a little longer than normal to process. Our priority at this time is the health and welfare of our staff and we ask that anyone visiting our site please wears a mask on arrival.

Following the Governments recent travel ban there has been an sharp increase in the volume of deliveries going to Tier 4 areas. As a consequence, our couriers have notified us that as from Tuesday 22nd December we will be unable to book on any further consignments bound for Tier 4 postcodes. We hope that when we return after the Christmas holidays things will have returned to normal and we apologise for any inconvenience that this may cause.

We are already experiencing challenges with deliveries across the whole of the distribution network and as the volume of orders increase in the run up to Christmas, we expect this to become worse. Some carriers aren’t guaranteeing next day service, whilst others are removing timed and weekend deliveries. With this in mind, where possible, please get your orders into us as early as possible, ideally giving a 48 hour window for delivery.
We’ll continue to ship same day for orders received by 4.00pm but please beware of potential delays.
With Lockdown 2 looming we are aiming to continue to operate like we did the whole way through the first lockdown, on a pretty much normal basis albeit still with reduced staffing.

The health and well being of our staff is of the utmost importance to us and we encourage anybody visiting our site to maintain their social distance and to use the hand sanitising stations that we have at each entrance.
As has been the case during these times, your order may take a little longer to be prepared than normal due to our reduced staffing level.

We are pleased to be open on a pretty much normal basis. We are observing strict social distancing rules and would ask that if you would like to collect your order that you order with us in advance to avoid unnecessary delays.
While on site you will be encouraged to use the hand sanitising stations that we have at each entrance.

Now that non-essential business’s and retail stores are returning to work, our delivery partners are experiencing an influx of collection requests which is putting the system under increased pressure. Because of that we would ask our customers to order 2 days in advance where possible to allow for any possible delays.

We are slowly increasing our staff levels and trying to offer as normal a service as possible. We have put lots of measures in place to protect the safety of our team. These include a one way system through our offices and warehouse so please bear with us if it takes a bit longer for us to answer the phone. At least we'll be fitter when we return to normal!!!

To enable us to pick, pack and despatch our daily orders we are having to reduce the hours that our telephones are manned. We will now be switching to night service at 4pm Mon-Thurs and 1pm on Fridays.
We have had to reduce our staffing levels even further and this will undoubtedly have an impact on our service.
We have had to remove the option for you to upgrade your order to a timed delivery.
All contact messages from our website and emails ending @dorotape.co.uk are being monitored but our response may be delayed due to these restrictions.

Phone calls to our main office number 01858 431642 may be diverted to a mobile number so in the event of any problems getting through, please leave a message and someone will contact you as soon as possible.

We are now working with a minimum number of staff and we ask that you please bear us and our delivery partners during these unprecedented times as your delivery make take longer than normal to reach you.

To best protect the health and safety of our colleagues and to maintain our social distancing, we are now working with about 50% of the number of staff. This has enabled those colleagues who also look after elderly family members, friends or neighbours or who have young children of their own can make sure that they have all they need in these difficult times.
The health and well being of our staff is of the utmost importance to us and as part of our duty of care we have put extra precautions into place to best protect their safety.
All non-essential travel has stopped and all non-essential visits cancelled.
We have provided extra hygiene products for staff and visitors with advise on their required usage.
All handles, taps, touch-pads and commonly touched surfaces are often wiped down with anti-bacterial wipes or sprays.
All deliveries and collections will be carried out on a non-contact basis meaning that you will not be asked to sign any paperwork.

In terms of stock holding, we are working very closely with our manufacturing partners in Europe and across the Globe to ensure that there will be no interruptions to supply and that we maintain our high standard of service to our customers.
We will be monitoring the situation closely as it develops in the coming days and weeks and we will keep you informed of our position if anything changes.
Thank you for your understanding and for your valued custom! We hope that you and your families remain well.

The ASTM E84 test is a standard of the American Society of Testing and Materials that measures the burning properties, or fire resistance of building materials that may be exposed to flames. The results can be classified according to three catergories, with Class A or I being the most fire resistant:
• Class A or I - Flame spread index up to 25
• Class B or II - Flame spread index 26-75

This standard was introduced in an attempt to harminise all European tests. Each of these three classifications have their own scale giving a much more in-depth analysis to the fire behaviour of the material.

font-size:120%"">We have put this information together to help anyone involved with floor graphics to understand the different slip resistance ratings as well as how

column1: our selection of floor graphic media fits in to those ratings.

We offer a wide range of floor graphic vinyl and non-slip laminates with different slip resistance ratings as well as floor marking tapes to help maintain social distancing for both indoor and outdoor use.

Our extensive printable floor graphic range includes two part floor graphic products ie: printable floor vinyl with a matching anti slip laminate as well as one part floor graphic textured printable vinyl solution.

With floor vinyl materials specifically suited for application to indoor smooth floors and carpets as well as for outdoor smooth and rough surfaces, we have the complete solution for your customer’s needs.

The R scale is a rating under DIN 51130 classification for shod feet that measures the slipperiness of a flooring surface. The 'R' stands for 'Ramp' and many European products are tested to this standard. The Ramp is adjustable so that the angle of slope can be raised, which when combined with a contaminant such as oil or a soap solution gives an increasingly slippery surface and the more likelihood that the test subject who is walking down the slope will slip. As soon as the ‘slip’ happens the ‘R’ is recorded. The steeper the angle of ramp when the slip happens the higher the R rating.
The ramp declination angles for each rating are set at:

As you can see from this, the R scale starts at R9 which is the lowest rating and progresses through increasing values to the highest floor slip resistance at R13. It is important to note that surfaces that are classified by the DIN 51130 standard as R9 and R10 will still be slippery when used in wet or greasy conditions.
• R9 should only be used in dry areas as it is still slippery when wet
• R10 should be only used in areas that are kept mainly dry but can be subject to spillages etc
• R11 can be used in areas that become wet more frequently such as reception or entrance areas of buildings and for short term outdoor use
• R12 can be used in wet areas and outdoors
• R13 is suitable for ramped areas that may become wet

Those products suitable to be used outdoors in wet conditions can also be rated under the DIN 51097 classification for use with bare feet. The rating is a simple A to C with A being the lowest and C being required for use in areas such as swimming pools, leisure centre changing rooms etc.

The Pendulum test is a classification under EN-13036 (similar to BS 7976-2) and instead of a ramp this test replicates a heel striking the floor using a swinging pendulum on level floors with no slope in both dry and wet conditions.

The PTV (Pendulum Test Values) are listed in a scale from 0 to 100 with 100 being the most slip resistant. The minimum slip resistance value considered safe for walking on in wet conditions is 36 PTV.
• 0 – 24 PTV indicates a high risk of slipping and is the approximate equivalent to R9
• 25 – 35 PTV indicates a moderate slip risk and is roughly the same as R10
• 36 – 74 PTV ratings suggest a low slip risk equivalent to R11 / R12
• A PTV value of more that 75 signifies an extremely low risk of slipping and can be thought of in the same way as R13

Peel adhesion tests, where the force required to peel the media defines how strong the adhesive is are commonly used for self-adhesive vinyl and films. The results can be catergorised as:
<ul><li>Removable adhesive = <19N/25mm<sup>2</sup>. These low tack films remain easy to remove after application without leaving an adhesive residue.
<li>Permanent adhesive = 20-28N/25mm<sup>2</sup>. Films with a permanent adhesive will be difficult to remove after application without leaving a residue.
Adhesion failure results in delamination of the film and adhesive from the substrate.
Adhesives come in various forms and each vinyl or film will have the right adhesive properties to match the material characteristics:
• Hot Melt - These adhesives, as the name suggests react to heat:
• PU hotmelt adhesives are primarily used for garment decoration films where the process of transferring the film to the material uses a heat press to activate the melting point.

• Rubber hotmelt adhesives are an economical coating for certain single and double sided tapes. The coating process involves heating the adhesive to melting point and coating it as a hot liquid, this means that these tapes are only to be used in areas not subjected to heat and direct sunlight as this would cause the rubber adhesive to dry out, turn yellowish and become brittle.

• UV Curable adhesives off a very high level of UV, heat and water resistance and while they have a high level of cohesion, while offering sometimes useful lower level of adhesion. UVC adhesives offer complete residue free removability.

• Solvent based adhesives have the benefit of a high degree of transparency as well as being water and solvent resistant. This makes them suitable for wet application but they also tend to be the most expensive type due to the extraction and disposal of the solvent gases from the drying process.

• Water based adhesives are sometimes referred to as dispersion adhesives as they are mixed with water to form an emulsion. The coating process is similar to solvent based adhesives except the water vapour released during the drying stage can simply be exhausted out of the production plant. As water based adhesives can re-emulsify when they come in to contact with moisture care has to be taken if applying wet as this can cause a slight milkiness effect.

column1: Calendered films are the most commonly used type by signmakers and large format printers. They start life as solid granules that are melted and compounded with heat and pressure in a mixing unit. This is then extruded, being drawn through a series of temperature controlled rollers which stretches and flattens it to a uniform thickness
column4: . Calendered films come in two main catergories

column1: Cast films are made differently to calendered films, starting off as a liquid which is then poured onto a casting sheet before moving slowly through a set of temperature controlled ovens where the liquid evaporates leaving behind an extremely thin layer. This then gets rolled
column4: . Cast films have little internal tension and are dimensionally stable, so shrinkage is barely perceptible. Cast films are thinner and softer, they are highly flexible and easier to apply over 3D curved surfaces using heat. With a durability in excess of 10 years, cast vinyl offers ultimate durability.

column1: CMYK stands for Cyan, Magenta, Yellow and Black (K stands for key as it was the black plate that was called to key plate on old printing presses) and printers lay down these colours in layers of dots (see dpi below) to produce the colour that the eye will see. This mode is used for all litho and digital printing and as long as your artwork is created and saved with the colour set to CMYK, it will accurately translate what is on the screen to what comes out of the printer.
Printers cannot interpret RGB so if your artwork is not set to CMYK when it is sent to print, colours will probably look dull, muted or inaccurate.
Cohesion is the bonding of the particles within the adhesive that holds it together, gives it internal strength and prevents it from splitting and leaving a residue.
Shear adhesion tests are ideal for measuring the cohesive properties of a bond either horizontally or vertically which is commonly used for double sided tapes (See Fig.2 below).
Cohesion failure results in the physical separation of the adhesive which will leave a residue.

Some plastic films with a low surface energy can be made more receptive to printing inks, coatings and adhesives by passing the material through a corona treatment process. This modifies the surface energy to improve adhesion and is done during production by converting standard electricity into high frequency power and delivering it to the surface by means of a ceramic or metal electrode over an air gap.
The cutting force value is measured in grams (gf) and depends entirely on the material being cut and the angle of the blade being used. Here is a general guideline:
DPI stands for Dots per Inch and refers to the amount of printed dots in an inch of the print. The larger the DPI, the higher number of dots and the clearer the print will be.

Usually, the higher the DPI, the higher quality of print and this is important for large format graphics but it is not always necessary to print at the highest DPI. If the print is small, using a high DPI may just be a waste of ink and might result in poor drying times.
This stands for 'grams per square metre' and is the weight measure for various non-adhesive flexible media such as paper, canvas and banner.

A typical 75µ vinyl is therefore thinner than one tenth of a mm.

Monomeric grade PVC is the most economical and least durable, best suited to interior and short-term exterior applications (4 years for Black & White, 3 years for colours) on to flat 1D and slightly curved 2D surfaces.

The monomeric plasticisers used in their production to make the film softer and more flexible have a low molecular weight which after time, slowly migrates to the surface of the film causing it to shrink and become brittle. These films are therefore not suitable for demanding exterior applications such as vehicle graphics or fascia signage as it will almost certainly start shrink back from the edges to reveal the adhesive beneath. Once this starts, any dirt in the atmosphere will quickly create a dirty grey outline around the graphics and eventually, the vinyl will begin to flake off like peeling paint.

The offset value is the distance from the centre of the blade to the cutting edge of the blade and is specified by the manufacturer of the blade. The offset determines the blade's turning radius and how it compensates for distance while turning corners.
A term used to describe how light is either blocked or passes through a vinyl or film. For our industry is can be broken down to:

• Blockout refers to a vinyl or film with zero transparency or translucence, meaning no light will pass through the material. This makes it suitable for use to block light out on windows as well as for use on to coloured substrates to prevent any show through.

• Opaque vinyl or film blocks out most natural light and are impossible to clearly see through (however we do find that some colours will be more opaque than others). With little or no transparency or translucence, opaque vinyl and films are the most commonly used type for signage and displays.

• Translucent films will allow light to pass through but it would be impossible to see clearly what is on the other side. Coloured translucent vinyl and films are used for glass decoration and printable translucent films are often used for backlit signage.

• Transparent vinyl and films allow light to pass through without interference making it easy to see through to the other side. Coloured transparent vinyl and films are used for glass and window decoration.

Polymeric grade vinyl uses polymeric plasticisers that have a more complex molecular chain meaning that they shrink back at a slower rate. This makes them more durable and with better UV and temperature resistance, suitable for longer term use outdoors on 1D and 2D surfaces (10 years for Black & White, 8 years for colours). If used on more complex curves, it is still recommended to cut and overlap seams as opposed to heating a stretching like you can a cast film (see below).

Raster images are pixel based and are best used when printing non line art images such as photographs as it is possible to include chromatic graduation and complex composition. Raster files are resolution specific meaning that they are intended to be displayed at one specific resolution. Increasing the image size will result in a loss of quality with images looking jagged and decreasing the size will result in blurry less crisp images. Raster file types include TIFF, JPEG, GIF, PNG and BMP and are also the most common type of file for displaying web graphics on screen.

• Paper liners are typically a base kraft paper of between 90gsm - 140gsm that has either a clay coating which is commonly seen on sign making vinyl and stencil films or a PE coating which is more common on digital print media due to the higher level of moisture resistance. The coatings work as a receptive layer for the final layer which is the siliconisation.
• For those materials requiring a final high degree of transparency, the kraft paper is replaced with a clear PET film and with a PE coating as this is much smoother.
RGB stands for Red, Green and Blue and represents colours of light that is viewable on a screen or monitor making it perfect for use on website and digital advertising.

If a graphic file is sent to print using RGB colour mode it will look very different that if it was sent over in CMYK format. This is because the printer has to change the image to CMYK to be able to process it correctly so it is always recommended that when sending artwork to print that it is done in CMYK mode.
There are two factors that will determine how strong the adhesive needs to be to stick to a particular surface. These are the finish of the surface and the surface energy.

<ul><li>Basically, the smoother the surface, the easier it is to stick to, simply because there is a greater surface area contact. A textured surface therefore requires a higher stronger adhesive as there is less surface for the adhesive to stick to.

• Without getting too nerdy, surface energy is the measurement of how well an adhesive will stick to it. Every surface has an 'energy' and this is measured in 'dyne'. Basically, the higher the surface energy, the easier it will be to stick to. Imagine a newly waxed car bonnet. Rain water will bead and run off easily because the wax is creating a low surface energy so water cannot stick to it.
Glass has a high surface energy so is easy to stick to whereas polypropylene has a low surface energy so harder to stick to and requires high tack adhesive levels to acheive a bond.

Tack refers to the initial stickiness of the adhesive and indicates how quickly a bond is formed when brought into contact with the substrate. There are various factors than can influence initial tack such as the surface energy of the substrate and temperature.

Vector images are based on mathematical formula that define geometric curves, circle, polygons and lines. Because of this vector graphics are best used for line art graphics such as logos, icons, charts and text. They are much more versatile than raster graphics and flexible so that graphics can be resized indefinitely without the loss of quality. Vector file types include EPS, AI, PDF & SVG.

column3: font-size:120%"">Here are some helpful tips and tricks for when things don't quite go to plan

column1: <button class=""accordion"">I'm getting air bubbles when I apply the vinyl</button>

To avoid air bubbles, it is important to remove any trapped air beneath the surface of the vinyl. Whether the vinyl is applied using a dry or wet application method, this is best achieved by carefully squeegeeing outwards from the centre of the graphic.

When removing the application tape, it is equally important not to do this too soon after the graphic has been applied, and not too quickly. For best results, work at a slow and steady pace and peel the application tape back at 1800, rather than lifting it upwards at 900.
When applying vinyl to rougher surfaces, always use a soft squeegee or roller to help prevent air entrapment.

Newly painted vehicles should be left for at least 5–10 days after painting before graphics are applied. During this time, the paint continues to release solvents as it cures. If graphics are applied too quickly, these solvents can become trapped beneath the vinyl, causing bubbles and potentially affecting adhesive performance.

Some plastics, such as polycarbonates and acrylics, are prone to outgassing, which is the gradual release of trapped gases formed during the manufacturing process. These materials are often supplied with a protective surface film. If vinyl or film is applied immediately after this protective liner is removed, the released gases can become trapped beneath the vinyl, leading to bubbles or blistering. To minimise this risk, remove any protective film early in the sign‑
column2: making process and avoid exposing the material to high temperatures after application.

column1: For a full compatibility list please visit the Application Advice
<button class=""accordion"">I've noticed that the vinyl is tunnelling when I unroll it from the cardboard core</button>

Some vinyl materials and polyester films can be susceptible to slight delamination when being unrolled from the core and laid flat on a workbench. This issue is often more noticeable with metallised vinyls and films, as these materials are generally less flexible.

This effect, often referred to as tunnelling, typically begins at the edge of the roll and can gradually work its way towards the centre. If a roll has been stored horizontally without adequate support, tunnelling may develop at pressure points and can be more pronounced if the material has been wound very tightly.

To minimise this risk, we strongly recommend storing vinyl rolls vertically to avoid pressure points. It is also important to ensure that storage areas are not exposed to temperature fluctuations or excessive humidity, as both can contribute to delamination and tunnelling issues.
<button class=""accordion"">How do I clean off old adhesive marks before applying new vinyl?</button>
This should be done by using a solvent based adhesive remover such as Right Off which will remove all traces in under 2 minutes.
It is then good practice to give the substrate a final wipe down using an Isopropyl alcohol. This will leave the surface ready for the new graphics to be applied.
<button class=""accordion"">I'm seeing peeling, cracking or edge lift on some of my work</button>

The most important factor is selecting the most suitable film for the job. We have created two blogs to help explain this in more detail, but as as a general rule it's worth remembering that while cast vinyl can be worked into channels and recesses as well as around compound curves using heat, calendared vinyl should applied without putting the film under any stress.
Check out these blog posts for more detailed information Cast vs Calendered and Understanding Calendered Vinyl

It is also vital to promote good initial adhesive contact to prevent graphics from lifting or peeling. All surfaces should be thoroughly cleaned, dried, and wiped with Isopropyl alcohol before any graphics are applied.
In colder conditions, applying heat after installation can help to further enhance the adhesive bond.
For a full compatibility list please refer to our Application Advice page.
To prevent digitally printed vinyl from peeling after application, it is essential to allow a 72‑

column1: <button class=""accordion"">The vinyl is separating from it's liner as it feeds into my printer</button>
This issue is noticeable during printing, when a tunnel forms at the edge of the roll and gradually expands towards the centre.

It is typically caused by the printer temperature being set too high, often in an attempt to speed up ink drying. Excessive heat causes the face film to expand while the release liner remains stable, resulting in delamination.
The problem can be exacerbated if the roll is loaded into the printer after being stored in a cold environment, such as on a Monday morning following weekend storage.
To help prevent this, we recommend loosening the material slightly on the core (this can be done by hand) and allowing the roll to acclimatise in the print room overnight before printing.
<button class=""accordion"">There seems to be a faint watermark in my print</button>
This effect is typically observed towards each end of the media roll and may occur if the roll has been left stationary while loaded in the printer for an extended period, such as overnight.

The weight of the roll resting on the support rollers over this time can create pressure points through the material. When printing resumes, these pressure marks can result in an uneven surface, producing this random visual effect.
<button class=""accordion"">I'm seeing a slight banding during printing</button>
In general, printers should operate at slower speeds for high‑
column2: quality output, where larger volumes of ink are applied, and at faster speeds for lower&#8209
column3: quality printing, where less ink is used.

column1: Fine banding visible in the print can be caused by ink overspray resulting from incorrect media feed calibration, so it is important to ensure all setup parameters are correctly configured.
Wider banding may occur when printing with a low number of passes in high‑
column3: directional mode. Increasing the number of passes or switching to uni&#8209
column4: directional mode can help to minimise this effect.

column1: If banding is only visible in a single colour, this is more likely to indicate an issue with the corresponding print head. Running a nozzle or swatch test is recommended to confirm whether the print head is performing correctly and to determine if replacement may be required. In some cases, mechanical factors such as worn or failing dampers may also contribute and should be checked. Trying an alternative print profile is also advised, as this can sometimes resolve banding related to ink laydown or environmental sensitivity.

Cyan ink, in particular, is highly sensitive to static, which is a common contributor to banding. Maintaining good temperature control and appropriate humidity levels in the print environment can significantly reduce this issue. When printing images with a high cyan ink content, the use of a humidifier positioned near the printer can be beneficial. Printing in uni‑
column2: directional mode can also help to reduce banding related to static interference.

column1: Where the banding is significantly wider or more pronounced across all colours, the cause may be pressure marks or “flat spots” created by the roll being stored horizontally and unsupported at the core. Rolls should always be stored in their original packaging and kept upright, ideally on a suitable
<button class=""accordion"">The banner material doesn't feed into the printer properly</button>

If the banner material doesn’t feed properly, the cause is usually a mix of alignment issues, roller grip, tension problems. One of the most common factors is the weight of the roll itself. A heavy roll can create too much resistance against the printer’s friction‑
column2: feed system, especially on older models, making it difficult for the printer to pull the material forward smoothly.

column1: If the leading edge is curled, uneven, or wrinkled, the printer may struggle to grip it, so flattening or trimming the edge can help.
Inspect the feed path and clean the rollers with Isopropyl alcohol to restore proper grip, remove any debris, and ensure the pinch rollers apply even pressure across the width.
When loading the roll, square the leading edge, align it carefully with the guides, and allow the printer to pre‑
column2: feed a small amount so it can establish a straight path.

column1: If the roll’s weight is causing resistance, manually unwinding the required amount of material before printing allows the banner to feed without drag, which is often the simplest and most effective workaround.

Be aware that contour cutting into the printed area too soon can lead to excessive shrinkage of the vinyl face film once applied. Cutting freshly printed vinyl before it has fully dried may cause the film to contract, and laminating too early can trap solvents. Depending on the ink load, this may reduce the film’s adhesive strength or shorten its service life by preventing proper solvent evaporation.
If the drying process occurs after the vinyl has already been applied to the substrate, the trapped solvents can cause the film to shrink and lift at the edges.
<button class=""accordion"">I've got tiny specks appearing in the print</button>

If tiny specks appear in the printed output, the most common cause is particulate contamination on the media surface. Dust or debris from the print room environment can settle on the substrate before printing, disrupting normal ink deposition. This may cause ink to pool around the particle, creating a dark spot, or prevent ink from adhering altogether, resulting in a small white void. To resolve this issue, thoroughly clean the surrounding print area to reduce airborne contaminants, then dry‑
column2: wipe the media roll with a clean, Lint Free Cloth to remove any settled debris before reprinting. Ensuring the media path and handling surfaces remain clean will help prevent recurrence.

column1: <button class=""accordion"">My printed image appears pixelated or blurred</button>
If your printed image appears pixelated, soft, or blurred, the issue is typically related to the quality or resolution of the original digital file rather than the printer itself. Low‑
column2: resolution images, excessive upscaling, or aggressive editing can reduce the amount of usable detail available for output, causing visible pixel structure or loss of sharpness once printed.

column1: To achieve optimal results, ensure that the source file has a sufficiently high native resolution for the intended print size and that any editing preserves image clarity. When preparing artwork, always verify that the file meets recommended DPI specifications and avoid enlarging images beyond their effective resolution, as this will inevitably degrade print clarity.
<button class=""accordion"">Ink is pooling and not drying during printing</button>

If ink is pooling on the surface of the media or failing to dry during printing, the issue is typically related to excessive ink laydown combined with insufficient drying time, which becomes especially noticeable on areas of dense, dark colour. Gloss surfaces are particularly prone to this, as they offer minimal absorption and rely heavily on correct print speed and curing times.
This effect often occurs when the printer is operating too quickly to allow solid colours to build correctly, causing wet ink to accumulate rather than settle.
To correct the problem, verify that the appropriate media profile and settings have been selected, reduce the carriage speed, increase the number of passes, or switch to Uni‑
column2: Directional printing to improve ink control and drying consistency.

column1: If the issue continues, consider reprinting the job on a matt vinyl or paper stock, which naturally absorbs more ink, and then apply a gloss laminate if a high‑
column2: sheen finish is required. This approach provides a faster&#8209
column3: drying alternative while maintaining the desired final finish.

column1: When printing onto transparent or translucent materials, the colours can appear washed out. This is because they lack the white base that normally supports and brightens printed colours, so the ink appears more see‑
column2: through. In addition, whatever sits behind the graphic—such as a window, wall, or bright daylight—can influence how the colours appear, often making them look weaker or uneven.

column1: To counter this, we would recommend overprinting the artwork again to double the amount of ink and colour depth. Overprinting simply means running the same design through the printer a second time so an additional layer of ink is applied directly on top of the first to give a more opaque colour.
<button class=""accordion"">I'm getting uneven colours when printing</button>
Uneven colour across the width of the roll is usually more noticeable when printing light or pastel tones because these colours rely on very subtle, low‑
column2: density ink coverage. Any small variation in how the print head lays down ink can show up as faint banding or shifts in colour from one side of the print to the other. This can happen when the print head moves too quickly or when bi&#8209
column3: directional printing introduces slight alignment differences between left&#8209

column1: To minimise this happening, it is recommended to switch printing to uni‑
column2: directional mode or reducing the print head speed.

column1: <button class=""accordion"">How long should I wait before laminating after printing?</button>
The amount of time you should wait before laminating large‑
column2: format prints depends mainly on the type of ink your printer uses. For solvent and eco&#8209
column3: solvent printers, a full 48 hours is generally the safest drying period. These inks release solvents as they cure, and laminating too soon can trap those vapours, leading to problems like bubbling, silvering, or poor adhesive bonding.

column2: based) inkjet prints dry through evaporation, so the wait time can vary more. Lightly saturated prints may be ready in as little as six hours, while heavily inked or photo&#8209
column3: quality prints often benefit from waiting closer to a full day or even longer. Allowing the moisture to dissipate fully helps prevent cloudiness or adhesion issues once the laminate is applied.

column1: Latex prints are much more forgiving because the ink is cured inside the printer. In most cases, they can be laminated almost immediately. It would be recommended to still give them an hour to settle, which helps ensure the surface is fully stable and the laminate bonds cleanly.

column2: cured prints also cure instantly, but because the ink sits on top of the media, laminating too quickly can sometimes cause silvering. They can be laminated right away, but waiting an hour tends to give better results, especially with laminates designed specifically for UV prints.

column1: Overall, the key reason for waiting is to avoid trapping uncured solvents or moisture beneath the laminate. Doing so can cause long‑
column2: term issues like tunnelling, delamination, or colour shifts. Giving the print the right amount of time to stabilise ensures a cleaner finish and a more durable final product.

column1: <button class=""accordion"">Some darker areas of my print have a silver sheen to them since I laminated it</button>

This effect is called silvering and appears as a faint metallic sheen in darker areas of a laminated print. It happens when tiny air pockets become trapped between the print surface and the adhesive layer of the laminate. These micro‑
column2: bubbles scatter light, which is why the effect is far more noticeable in deep blacks and rich colours rather than in lighter tones. The most common cause is laminating at too low a temperature—either because the laminator hasn’t fully warmed up or because the film itself is running cooler than it needs to be. When the adhesive isn’t warm enough to flow and bond properly, it can’t displace the air, so the bubbles remain suspended beneath the film.

column1: Applying heat to the rollers during application, typically around 40
column2: °C, allows the adhesive to soften and activate. As it warms, it flows more evenly across the print surface, pushing out the trapped air.

column1: If the film is applied with heat, the effect may diminish slightly over time as the adhesive slowly settles, but it usually won’t disappear completely.

Ensuring the laminator reaches the correct operating temperature before starting, and maintaining consistent heat throughout the run, is the most reliable way to prevent silvering from occurring in the first place.
<button class=""accordion"">I'm getting a lot of electrostatic charge build up</button>
Electrostatic charge is an unavoidable part of working with self‑
column2: adhesive films, and it’s mainly generated when the release liner is peeled away from the adhesive. The friction created during this separation builds static electricity, and the faster the liner is removed, the stronger that charge becomes. This static can attract dust, interfere with how smoothly the film lays down, and even affect the person applying it.

column1: Several conditions influence how noticeable this charge becomes, and there are practical ways to minimise its impact. A dust‑
column2: free environment is essential, as static naturally pulls airborne particles toward the adhesive. Cleaning the workspace just before application helps reduce contamination. Humidity also plays a major role: dry air increases static buildup, while higher humidity suppresses it. Something as simple as placing a bowl of water in the room can help, as the evaporating moisture reduces airborne dust and lowers static levels. Lightly misting the air before removing the liner can have a similar effect by adding moisture and helping particles settle.

column1: The person applying the film can also accumulate static, which may disrupt the application process. Touching a grounded metal object before handling the film helps discharge this buildup safely. When using a laminator—especially at higher speeds—static can accumulate even more quickly. In these cases, grounding the machine with anti‑
column2: static devices can prevent sudden shocks and reduce the likelihood of static&#8209

If your vinyl isn’t cutting correctly—and you’re seeing problems such as difficult weeding, rounded corners, lifting edges, or cuts that don’t go all the way through—the most common cause is incorrect blade setup. Even small issues with blade depth, pressure, or offset can have a noticeable impact on cut quality.
Below is a basic summary of cutter blade design including details about blade angle and offset value which have a big impact on how well your blade is cutting.

The offset value (typically 0.5 ± 0.05, as shown above) refers to the distance between the centre of the blade and the blade tip. This value is set by the blade manufacturer and determines how the cutter compensates when turning corners. In other words, the offset controls the blade’s turning radius and ensures accurate, clean cuts on curves and sharp angles.
The diagram above shows a 55o blade. For most standard sign‑

Correct blade setup is essential, regardless of the blade angle. The blade extension is adjusted by twisting the cap on the blade holder, and you should always use the minimum extension needed to cut the material cleanly. One of the most common causes of poor cutting performance is having the blade extended too far.

A reliable way to set the correct extension is to begin with the blade protruding to roughly half the thickness of a credit card. Perform a test cut and assess the result. If the cut does not penetrate the material properly, increase the cutting force first. Only increase the blade extension if additional force alone is not sufficient.

<button class=""accordion"">Why is the vinyl not releasing from its backing liner</button>
It’s easy to assume that application tape isn’t tacky enough to lift cut and weeded graphics, but this is rarely the true cause.
In most cases, the issue is excessive blade pressure during cutting, which causes the blade to score too deeply into the backing liner.

To diagnose this, peel back a section of the cut vinyl and check the liner. The blade should only lightly mark the surface—there should be no deep scoring. Then inspect the reverse side of the liner. If you can see impressions of the cut path showing through, the pressure is too high. Reduce the cutting pressure gradually and run several test cuts until you achieve the correct setting. Once the pressure is optimised, the graphics should lift cleanly and easily.

For the best results when removing graphics from the liner, avoid pulling the application tape away from the vinyl. Instead, flip the graphic over and peel the backing liner away from the adhesive side. This method reduces stress on the vinyl and improves transfer success.

<button class=""accordion"">How can I remove old vinyl?</button>
The most effective way to remove self‑
column2: adhesive vinyl is by applying heat. A hairdryer or heat gun can be used to raise the temperature to around 200oC, but take care not to overheat the material, as excessive heat can cause the vinyl to melt rather than soften.

column1: Once the vinyl is warm and pliable, lift a corner carefully and begin peeling it back slowly at a 180o angle. Pulling the film flat along the surface reduces the risk of damaging the substrate underneath. Avoid pulling at a 90o angle, as this increases the chance of lifting paint, laminate, or other finishes.

After the vinyl has been removed, some adhesive residue may remain. This can usually be cleaned off with an adhesive remover such as Right-Off Cleaner in addition to an appropriate tool such as Scraperite Soft Surface Scraper.

<h2 style= ""text-align:center"">A Decade of High-Impact Design at London Fashion Week<span style=""color:#009fe3

The Graphical Tree, a long-standing specialist in graphics and signage, has worked across London Fashion Week for nearly a decade. Held at The Store Studios on the Strand, the event demands high-impact visual elements that can transform large, whitewashed spaces into immersive, photo-ready environments.

Working in close partnership with creative production agency Blonstein, The Graphical tree needed materials that could act as the star of the show—creating statement backdrops, enhancing wayfinding, and supporting designer branding, while remaining flexible enough to change season after season.

Dichroic film, supplied by Dorotape, became a consistent and defining feature of the London Fashion Week installations. Supplied in various forms over the years, the material was used to create striking backdrops through cut lettering, custom shapes, and full dichroic wall and glass applications. Its colour-shifting properties delivered the visual impact required for key feature walls, reception areas, and designer spaces. Many of which became popular photo backdrops for guests and attendees.

A standout application was seen during Autumn 2017, where premium dichroic vinyls were specified, including the transparent ASLAN SE70 Nebula dichroic film on glass and ASLAN SE71 Aurora dichroic opaque film on walls, producing dramatic, light-reactive effects. Alongside this, hundreds of cut vinyl elements were produced each season for designer names, directories, and wayfinding, ensuring consistency across all signage.

Thanks to Blonstein’s detailed briefings, our material suggestions, production methods, and installation schedules were carefully planned in advance, allowing seamless installation and efficient changeovers—particularly when the venue transitioned from London Fashion Week to London Fashion Week Festival.

The repeated use of dichroic material has helped shape the evolving visual identity of London Fashion Week, delivering bold, memorable environments that captivate guests year after year. The combination of premium materials, precise execution, and long-term collaboration has ensured maximum impact while supporting the fast-paced demands of one of the fashion calendar’s most important events.

<h2 style= ""text-align:center"">Wildkicks Studio packs a punch with JW Signs and Dorotape<span style=""color:#009fe3

With the brand-new opening of Wildkicks, a space dedicated to fitness through Thai Boxing, strength and conditioning training and Pilates, Shane at JW Signs was tasked with printing a large wall mural going centre stage in the recently refurbished fitness studio.

Owner of Wildkicks, Alex Munro wanted something big and bold to be applied on to the painted surface right next to the main fitness area. Understanding the demands of such a tough environment, Shane knew it was super important that the correct printable vinyl was selected so he contacted Dorotape to discuss the project.

Although Dorotape had several suitable vinyl options, there was only one material that ticked all the boxes, making it the perfect choice for the job. ASLAN DFP08G is a polymeric grade vinyl with a non-reflective matt white finish that prevents glare from ceiling downlights, an ultra-high tack adhesive that bonds well to uneven surfaces and a grey pigment in the adhesive giving it a high level of opacity.

The last consideration was the ink compatibility to the Roland TrueVis VG2 640 that JW Signs recently invested in and again ASLAN DFP08G was the ideal choice. With exceptional print quality, ASLAN DFP08G was printed in one hit, laminated with Poli-Print 1235 Transparent Matt laminate before being applied with ease to the wall, transforming the fitness studio a truly professional look and ambience.

<h2 style= ""text-align:center"">Wrapping History: A Landmark Transformation in Northampton<span style=""color:#009fe3

In 2025, Northampton Town Council launched a year-long programme of events to mark the 350th anniversary of the Great Fire of Northampton. At the centre of the celebrations stood the town’s main church, a landmark rich in history and significance.

The organisers wanted this iconic building to become a bold focal point for the commemorations. The challenge was clear: the installation needed to be visually striking and durable, yet completely non-invasive, leaving the centuries-old church stonework untouched.

Commercial Print House, Tangerine Red developed a daring yet sensitive design concept to transform the church into the centrepiece of the event. Struggling to find a suitable material for such a unique application, the team turned to Dorotape for advice. We recommended Kernow Ultimate Lightblock 230STL Textured Roll-Up Film - a lightweight material renowned for its strength, stability, and ability to achieve a flawless fit especially when applied to a curved surface such as church columns.
Printed with UV inks on a Mimaki UCJV300-160, the material delivered everything the project required:
• Zero mechanical fixings - ensuring no damage to the heritage stone
• Seamless, solid fit - enhancing the impact of the design
• Durability - withstanding the elements for a year long installation

The finished installation blends creativity with heritage, vividly bringing the story of the Great Fire to life in the heart of the town. The bold wrap became not just a visual spectacle, but also an engaging way to share historical insight with the community.

“Using this material was a risk but we were assured by Dorotape that the material would work for the special application we had for this material. Our customer was so happy with the finish and was grateful we could apply this in the dreadful weather conditions that we faced – it performed perfectly.”

Sustainability isn’t a bolt-on initiative at Dorotape - it’s embedded in how we operate every day.

From supporting our team and local community to reducing our environmental impact, we place sustainability at the heart of our decision-making. Every operational choice is considered through the lens of environmental responsibility.

column2: >Good Business Charter accredited business, we believe doing the right thing should be standard practice. By putting people and planet first, we demonstrate that ethical governance, fair treatment and environmental responsibility are not just good principles, they are good business.

column1: Our GBC DNA

Our commitment to the planet goes far beyond words. We have worked with the University of Leicester through its Climate Leadership Programme to become Carbon Literate, strengthening our understanding of the climate challenge and our role within it. We have also collaborated with the SME Climate Hub initiative, reinforcing our commitment to a net-zero future.
• Clear actions to achieve a 50% reduction in emissions by 2030

We have already implemented meaningful changes in relation to climate mitigation. These include the installation of LED lighting across our office and warehouse spaces, with motion sensors to reduce unnecessary energy consumption in certain areas, roof re-insulation to minimise heat loss, and EV charging points to support lower-emission transport.
Our Carbon Reduction Plan
Net-zero vs carbon neutral: what's the difference

Carbon neutral can be achieved by paying a fee to offset an organisation's carbon emissions. Net-Zero calls for internal reductions in a carbon footprint to be made, and for the residual emissions to be offset through credible carbon removal projects.
Our focus is firmly on reduction first, residual offsetting second as we continue to work towards net-zero emissions by 2050.
Individual action matters. Collective action transforms industries.

While recycling at home is important, the real opportunity lies in reshaping how our sector operates. The graphics and materials industry has significant influence and therefore significant responsibility.
For many years, Dorotape has positioned itself at the forefront of offering more sustainable material alternatives. We work closely with global manufacturing partners to source and supply:

But supply alone is not enough. Education is equally important. We actively share knowledge from manufacturers’ R&D teams with our customers, helping them understand material choices, lifecycle impact and practical application. When our customers are better informed, they are better equipped to make more sustainable decisions - and unlock new commercial opportunities in the process.
We believe sustainability should be collaborative. By working together across the supply chain, we can accelerate meaningful change for our industry.
